F32 — NOTICE line 95 still reads json, html, css and javascript grammars only, while ancora.review.prism_carried now says markup. The vendored file is prism-markup.min.js, which registers the markup grammar and aliases html, xml, svg, mathml, rss, atom and ssml; Prism ships no prism-html.min.js. Reword NOTICE and the requirement so they agree and both state what is true: core Prism supplies markup, css and javascript, and these seven component files supply the rest. review_assets_test.exs only checks that NOTICE contains the string PrismJS 1.29.0, so nothing catches this drift.
F62 — five of the six priv/spec_init templates carry a .eex extension with no tags in them, yet all six go through EEx.eval_file, so a future literal opening EEx tag in that markdown would crash or evaluate. Rename the five tag-free templates to plain .md and .yml and copy them with File.cp!, keeping EEx.eval_file for AGENTS.md.eex alone, which has the one real tag.
F64 — republish the 30-code table in docs/migration.md with a default-severity column. The broader config-schema and Spec-Ack grammar documentation is deliberately NOT taken here.
F66 — give Git.read_blob/2 no-port fallback the same stderr separation the batch port has, so a git warning cannot be prepended into blob content. Add a comment at base_view.ex:52 recording that path-traversal safety depends on read_blob resolving through the git rev-colon-path form, so a future bulk-read optimization does not silently remove it. The security reviewer built a working proof-of-concept for that traversal: git mktree does accept a dot-dot entry and ls-tree -r emits it, and the chain reaches BaseView.materialize through a hostile default_base, but every blob read goes through rev-colon-path and git refuses to resolve dot-dot, so it dies before any write. The defense is real and undocumented.

There are EIGHT files matching priv/spec_review_assets/prism-*.min.js: css, diff, elixir, erlang, json, markdown, markup, yaml. The omitted one is prism-markup.min.js, the exact file F32 was filed about. TWO THINGS I GOT WRONG, corrected here so you do not inherit them:

1. I wrote that review_assets_test.exs cross-checks NOTICE against the requirement and has no filesystem derivation. That is not right. Line 24-25 already reads the directory with Path.wildcard, lines 39-42 pin the exact ten filenames, and lines 44-45 pin all ten digests. The directory IS pinned. What is missing is any assertion connecting a prose sentence to that listing. So DO NOT BUILD A SECOND DERIVATION. `files` already exists at line 24 and the remedy is about eight lines on top of it.

2. I offered two readings of the ambiguous sentence and told you to choose one. Both are wrong, so do not choose either. The sentence's premise is unsatisfiable: prism.min.js already registers markup, css, javascript and clike, so prism-css.min.js and prism-markup.min.js DUPLICATE core rather than supplying anything beyond it. There is no true version of a core-versus-components split here.

The fix is to delete the split, not to repair it. The base wording at 7511407 was already correct and simple, one enumeration of the trimmed grammar set. Return to that, with clike added because core registers it and the old wording mildly under-claimed. The audit comment gives the exact text for NOTICE, the requirement, the scenario, and the ADR.

F32 and Behaviors-to-demonstrate (2) above still say "the seven component files supply the rest". Read that whole clause as void, not just the number. "Supply the rest" is the half that cannot be made true under any count, which is why correcting the count alone would have shipped a third false sentence in the same paragraph.

The real deliverable is falsifiability, not wording. Today, adding prism-ruby.min.js or dropping markup from NOTICE breaks nothing. After the fix, both fail. Do not add a cross-check against the html.ex load list: html.ex is Out of Scope (files), and parsing source from a test is exactly the machinery this epic exists to shed. Directory derivation is the deliverable.

Out of Scope (intent) above says "no removal of the seven component grammars". Read that as eight. It guards against deleting grammars and it still stands.

The ticket's premise, that git refuses to resolve dot-dot through the rev-colon-path form, does not hold on git 2.49.0. I built the tree by hand with plumbing and ran it:
  - `git mktree` accepts an entry named `..` at any depth, and `git ls-tree -r` emits the joined path. Both match the ticket's account.
  - `git show <rev>:sub/..` returns the blob with exit 0. `git show <rev>:a/../../evil.txt`, built from three nested trees whose entries are named `..`, also returns the blob with exit 0. `git cat-file --batch` resolves both identically, so the batch port path is affected too, not just the no-port fallback.

With TMPDIR pinned to a sandbox, the root was <sandbox>/tmp/ancora_base_view_31716_2018 and the file landed at <sandbox>/tmp/evil.txt. Path.join/2 does not normalize `..`, File.mkdir_p! creates the intermediate `a` so the OS resolves the traversal, and File.write! follows it out.
  - Reachable from the gate: BaseView.materialize is called at lib/ancora/gate.ex:67 and lib/ancora/review.ex:41, via the same hostile-default_base chain the ticket already accepts.

ORCHESTRATOR NOTE before audit: I reproduced part of this and could NOT reproduce the decisive part (2026-09-03 21:10). Routing to audit rather than acting on it, and NOT reporting a vulnerability to Manuel until it is settled.

What I confirmed, on git 2.49.0, in a scratch repo:
- git mktree ACCEPTS a tree entry literally named '..'. It does not reject it.
- git ls-tree -r emits the joined path, so BaseView would iterate an entry whose path is 'a/..' or '../evil.txt'.
- git cat-file --batch RESOLVES '<commit>:a/..' and returns the blob header and payload, exit 0.

So the comment added at lib/ancora/base_view.ex:67-68 is FALSE as written. Git does not reject tree entries containing '..' before this code writes them. That alone justifies the FAIL, and it is what this ticket's own instruction called a Gap rather than a Note.

What I could NOT reproduce is the escape itself, which is the part that would make this a security issue rather than a documentation defect:
- I built a top-level tree entry named '..' containing evil.txt. ls-tree -r emits '../evil.txt', exactly the shape that would escape on write, and Path.join('/tmp/ancora-base-ROOT', '../evil.txt') does expand to /tmp/evil.txt.
- But git cat-file --batch REFUSES that path: 'fatal: ../evil.txt is outside repository'. So the read never returns content for the one path shape that would escape the write root.
- The form git DOES resolve, 'a/..', joins to root/a/.. which expands back to the root itself, a directory. File.write! there fails rather than escaping.

So on my evidence the two properties do not line up: the paths git will read do not escape, and the path that would escape git will not read. I may be missing the combination that does both. A three-level shape like 'a/../../evil.txt' is the obvious candidate and I did not construct it.

AUDITOR: settle this, and be specific about which of us is wrong. The verifier states it ran the real production functions and observed materialize/2 write a file one directory above its own root. If that is right, my reproduction is incomplete and I want the exact tree shape and the exact read that succeeded. If it is wrong, say so plainly: this epic has already had three claims disproved by re-measurement, and a false security report costs more than a missed one here because it would go to Manuel as a vulnerability.

Either way the FAIL stands on the comment alone. What the audit decides is the REMEDY, and that is a scope call:
